name: Orokaiva (Retired)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Larsen, Robert E. & Marlys Larsen. 1977. Orokaiva phonology and orthography. In R. Loving (ed.), Phonologies of five P.N.G. languages, 5-28. Ukarumpa: SIL.

new_statements.quote: Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word. If the first two syllables involve the sequence Va, then the second syllable sometimes seems to be nearly as prominent as the first one. In reduplicated and compound words a secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the second root. In simple words a secondary stress tends to occur on the third syllable, but it is not easily heard if that syllable does not contain a stop or /a/.
new_statements.citation: Larsen, Robert & Marlys Larsen. 1977. Orokaiva phonology and orthography. In Richard Loving (ed.), Phonologies of five P.N.G. languages (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 19), 5-28. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: printed p.12, section 5.1 'Stress' (PDF p.8 of the SIL-PNG scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened (symlink to../orok1269/, fetched sources 2026-09-16 from a Wayback id_ capture of the SIL-PNG pubs URL, item 928474523833) and rendered PDF p.8 = printed p.12 at 100 dpi; read the page image directly. Section '5 ALLOPHONES AND CONTRASTS / 5.1 STRESS' reads exactly: 'Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word. If the first two syllables involve the sequence Va, then the second syllable sometimes seems to be nearly as prominent as the first one. [para] In reduplicated and compound words a secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the second root. In simple words a secondary stress tends to occur on the third syllable, but…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-contrastive) and falls on the first syllable of every word; a rhythmic secondary stress tends to fall on the third syllable of simple words, and in compounds/reduplications on the first syllable of the second root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of the second root in reduplicated and compound words; in simple words it tends to fall on the third syllable (weakly audible unless that syllable has a stop or /a/). Larsen & Larsen 1982:77 restate this as 'second greatest emphasis is on the third syllable in words longer than two syllables'.
new_statements.exceptions: When the first two syllables form the sequence V + a, the second syllable 'sometimes seems to be nearly as prominent as the first one' (Larsen & Larsen 1977:12). No lexical exceptions given. Healey et al. 1969:34 add that enclitics (ra, re, rate, rami) are pronounced as part of the preceding word.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word ('each word'), including affixed verb words up to ten syllables listed in sec.3; vowels in monosyllables and stressed syllables tend to be lengthened (sec.5.2). Independent concurring statements: Healey, Isoroembo & Chittleborough 1969:34 (PL A-18) 'The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed.' (Isivita dialect) and Larsen & Larsen 1982:77 (WPNGL 30, Grammar Notes sec.1.3). Larsen's data: dialect spoken between Agenehambo and Wasida on the Popondetta-Kokoda road (Sui village), 1971-74, i.e. Orokaiva proper [okv] (Smallhorn 2011 calls the Larsens' variety the Sose/Western Plains dialect).
new_statements.identity_note: orok1270 'Orokaiva (Retired)' is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING languoid for ISO 639-3 [ork], retired 2008-01-14 (change request 2007-190) and split into Orokaiva [okv] = orok1269, Aeka [aez] = aeka1244 and Hunjara-Kaina Ke [hkk] = hunj1241. It is not a distinct language and must not be added as a separate catalog row (retired codes confer no identity). Orokaiva proper (orok1269) is ALREADY in the catalog, sourced to Healey, Isoroembo & Chittleborough 1969:34. All three first-hand statements found here (Larsen & Larsen 1977:12; Healey et al. 1969:34; Larsen & Larsen 1982:77) describe Orokaiva proper [okv]/orok1269: Larsen's data are from the Agenehambo-Wasida stretch of the Popondetta-Kokoda road (Sui village; Smallhorn 2011 labels the Larsens' variety the Sose / Western Plains dialect), Healey's from Isivita village. The Larsen & Larsen 1977 quote is the fuller, more authoritative primary phonology and should be attached to orok1269 (upgrading/corroborating the Healey 1969 citation), not to orok1270. The other daughters of the retired code are not covered: Smallhorn 2011:80 lists Hunjara (hunj1241) among penultimate-stress Binanderean languages, so the retired macro-code is prosodically heterogeneous; Aeka (aeka1244) has no stress statement in anything opened here.

sources.note: p.12 sec.5.1: stress non-phonemic; primary stress always on the first syllable of each word; secondary stress on first syllable of second root in reduplicated/compound words, and tends to fall on the third syllable in simple words; if first two syllables are V+a the second may be nearly as prominent. Dialect: Agenehambo-Wasida road (Sui village), i.e. Orokaiva proper [okv]. Verified on page image (PDF p.8).
